opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest mistake is believing that being smart means taking shortcuts. A lot of people, especially when they're young and do well in school, start to think intelligence is about finding the clever trick that lets them skip the hard part. Sometimes that works, but over time it becomes a trap.

What I've found is that the things that really matter, like building a good system, writing solid code, or understanding a problem deeply, usually don't have shortcuts. You have to do the boring, careful work. You have to read the documentation, write the tests, and think through edge cases. People who are "too smart" often avoid that because it feels beneath them, and then they end up with something fragile.

The second part of the mistake is trying to *look* smart instead of trying to *be* effective. If you care too much about appearing clever, you stop asking simple questions, you don't admit when you're confused, and you over-engineer things to impress people. In my experience, the most capable people I've worked with are very comfortable saying "I don't understand, can you explain it again?" They choose simple solutions whenever possible.

So I'd say real intelligence is mostly about judgment: knowing what's worth doing, being honest about what you don't know, and being willing to put in the unglamorous effort. Cleverness is a tool, not the goal.

r001.rationale: The response identifies shortcut-seeking and trying to look smart as mistakes, but does not say the mistake is prioritizing how to solve a problem over why to pursue it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest mistake is confusing being smart with looking smart. When I was younger, especially in school and early in grad school, a lot of my energy went into appearing clever: using the most sophisticated tool, picking the hardest-sounding problem, writing code that only I could read. That's actually a very expensive way to be dumb.

Real smartness, at least the kind that compounds, is mostly about choosing the right problem and then being willing to be embarrassingly simple about solving it. When we started Taichi, the "smart" move would have been to build a huge general-purpose compiler from day one. The actually smart move was to get one simulation running fast, show it to people, and let their feedback tell us what mattered. Most of the cleverness I'm proud of came from removing things, not adding them.

The second part of the mistake is optimizing for being right instead of for learning fast. If you need to be the smartest person in the room, you stop asking basic questions, and basic questions are where all the leverage is. I've learned more from saying "I don't understand, can you explain it like I'm new" than from any amount of pretending.

So if I had to compress it: don't try to be smart. Try to be useful and curious, and be honest about what you don't know. Smart tends to show up on its own after that.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes trying to look clever and emphasizes choosing the right problem, but it does not identify prioritizing how to solve a problem over why to pursue it as the biggest mistake.
